newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges supporters to ignore his surge in polls.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges supporters to ignore his surge in polls.

text.p: With unemployment dropping and opinion polls showing a surge in his support, President Bill Clinton on Friday urged his supporters to avoid taking "anyone's vote for granted" in the November election.

Hoping to end a two-decade-old Republican stranglehold over Florida's presidential voting, Clinton wrapped up a two-day swing through the state by stressing his record on the economy, education, the environment and health care -- areas where he has a solid edge over Republican rival Bob Dole.
With a series of new nationwide polls showing Clinton with a growing double-digit lead over his Republican challenger, the Democratic incumbent publicly cautioned his followers against complacency.
"Let me assure you, we are not taking anyone or anyone's vote for granted," he said in a speech to delegates at the National Baptist Convention, an 8 million-member black group.
"We know that the only poll that counts is the one they take on November the fifth," Clinton told the highly partisan audience. "I ask you to remember that and help others remember it as well."

In appearances before the Baptist group and later at Valencia Community College, he celebrated new unemployment figures that showed that the nation's jobless rate had dropped to 5.1 percent -- its lowest level in seven years.

"The American economy, my fellow Americans, is on the right track and we need to keep it going in that direction," said Clinton, who contends that the 15 percent across-the-board tax cut advocated by Dole would only reverse the nation's economic progress.

Clinton campaign officials privately have worried that overconfidence could undermine their efforts as the Nov. 5 election nears -- particularly now that some of the inroads Dole made at the time of last month's Republican convention have been eroding.

A Washington Post-ABC News poll published on Friday gave Clinton a lead of 51 percent to 37 percent over Dole, while a New York Times-CBS News survey the same day put the margin at 50 to 35 percent in favour of the incumbent.

A nationwide poll taken for Reuters found broad-based support for Clinton over his Republican rival on a series of issues that potential voters said was important to them. The poll, conducted by John Zogby International, found that on education issues 55.4 percent of voters favoured Clinton, 25.4 percent backed Dole and 6.2 percent trusted Texas billionaire Ross Perot, the Reform Party candidate.

On health care, Clinton was favoured by 48.7 percent to 27.7 percent for Dole, while Perot trailed with 5.2 percent. Clinton held a similar wide lead on dealing with environmental issues, with 51.1 percent of voters comfortable with him while 19.2 percent chose Dole. Perot was backed by 3.2 percent.
Clinton campaign officials said it was no coincidence the president was stressing those themes in his appearances. "We feel that our message is doing very well," campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart said.
Internal campaign polling shows Clinton slightly ahead in Florida, whetting his appetite to try to become the first Democratic candidate to win there since Jimmy Carter in 1976.

In Orlando, Clinton also attended a Democratic National Committee luncheon expected to raise $200,000. Later he planned to visit Panama City to speak at Gulf Coast Community College and attend a political reception before returning to Washington late on Friday night.
